y-m-54-01.title: Changing a friend's expression: can we trust it?
y-m-54-01.topic: An error in a solution that expands a squared expression, and the condition for it to hold
y-m-54-01.goal: Find the line that goes wrong in a solution that changed (x+3)² into x²+9, and discover with examples you make yourself in which cases the expression (a+b)²=a²+b² is right.
y-m-54-01.material: Minjun thought that (x+3)² can be changed into x²+9, and wrote his solution as below. x is a letter that stands for a real number. (x+3)² is read as 'x plus 3, the whole bracket squared.'
y-m-54-01.thinking.0: Checking the reason for each line of the solution
y-m-54-01.thinking.1: Noticing the limit of checking with a single value
y-m-54-01.thinking.2: Collecting examples where it holds and guessing the condition
y-m-54-01.prereq.0: This task assumes the difficulty assignment (H2) of the 'high school Basic Math 1 track' and does not indicate in which grade the content is learned (school arrangements vary). Middle school level calculation with letter expressions (distribution, the meaning of powers) and calculating squares of integers.
y-m-54-01.s.s1.prompt: Pick one line in Minjun's solution whose reasoning is not right. (Lines are counted from 1.)
y-m-54-01.s.s1.hint.0: Tell apart whether each line gives a reason for 'why it is so' or just makes a statement.
y-m-54-01.s.s1.hint.1: Pick a value other than the x=0 used in line 4 and do the same check yourself.
y-m-54-01.s.s1.line.0: (x+3)² is the expression (x+3) multiplied by itself twice.
y-m-54-01.s.s1.line.1: Multiplication can be distributed to the terms in the bracket, so the square also applies to x and to 3 separately.
y-m-54-01.s.s1.line.3: Check: if x=0, the left side is (0+3)²=9 and the right side is 0²+9=9, which are the same. So this expression is right.
y-m-54-01.s.s1.explain: There are problems in line 2 and line 4. Line 2: the square is not applied separately to the two terms in the bracket; in (x+3)(x+3), all pairs (x·x, x·3, 3·x, 3·3) appear. Line 4: because x=0 works for one value, we cannot say it works for all x. For example, if x=1, the left side is 16 and the right side is 10. (Choosing either one of the two is accepted as correct.)
y-m-54-01.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different integer pairs (a, b) for which (a+b)² = a²+b² really holds. Conditions: a and b are integers from -9 to 9, and the case where a and b are both 0 is excluded. (Pairs with a and b swapped count as the same example.)
y-m-54-01.s.s2.hint.0: First pick a few pairs like (1,2), (2,2), (0,3), calculate both sides of each, and write them in a table.
y-m-54-01.s.s2.hint.1: In the pairs where the two sides were equal, look for a shape that the values of a and b have in common.
y-m-54-01.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are integers from -9 to 9.
y-m-54-01.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers from -9 to 9.
y-m-54-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The two values are not equal. Calculate them directly and compare.
y-m-54-01.s.s2.explain: Since (a+b)²=a²+2ab+b², to be equal to a²+b² we need 2ab=0. So only the pairs where at least one of a and b is 0 are found. If you organize the pairs you tried in a table, this common feature is visible.
y-m-54-01.s.s3.prompt: Looking at the pairs you found in s2, pick the statement that best describes the cases where (a+b)² = a²+b² holds.
y-m-54-01.s.s3.hint.0: For each choice, make one pair that fits its condition and calculate both sides.
y-m-54-01.s.s3.hint.1: If even one pair satisfies the condition but does not match, that choice is not the condition for it to hold.
y-m-54-01.s.s3.o.a: It holds only when a and b are the same number
y-m-54-01.s.s3.r.a: You may have tested only a few examples with a=b and generalized. Put in something like (2,2) directly.
y-m-54-01.s.s3.o.b: It holds when at least one of a and b is 0
y-m-54-01.s.s3.r.b: This is a guess that organizes the shape that the examples found have in common into a condition.
y-m-54-01.s.s3.o.c: It holds when a and b are opposite numbers (sum 0)
y-m-54-01.s.s3.r.c: You may have looked only at the pairs with sum 0 gathered together. Even when the sum is 0, check whether the right side becomes different.
y-m-54-01.s.s3.o.d: It holds when a and b are both positive
y-m-54-01.s.s3.r.d: It does not hold even if you test just a few pairs of positive numbers. For example, put in (1,1).
y-m-54-01.s.s3.explain: In all the examples found, one of the numbers was 0, and since (a+b)²−(a²+b²)=2ab, if neither number is 0 they must not match. Therefore Minjun's expression is not a 'general rule' and is right only in special cases.

y-m-54-02.title: Harin's division: is it always fine?
y-m-54-02.topic: Number of solutions of a linear equation with a letter in the coefficient
y-m-54-02.goal: Learn that the number of solutions of an equation like (a-2)x=b-3 changes with a and b, judge what you need to know before stating the solution, and make a and b that fit the conditions yourself.
y-m-54-02.material: There is an equation (a-2)x = b-3 in x. a and b are numbers (constants) whose values are not yet decided. Harin said, “If you divide both sides by a-2, you get x=(b-3)/(a-2), so there is always one solution,” and Ujin said, “It can change depending on a.” (a-2)x is read as 'a minus 2, times x.'
y-m-54-02.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-54-02.thinking.1: Telling apart conclusions that change with conditions
y-m-54-02.thinking.2: Making examples that satisfy the conditions
y-m-54-02.prereq.0: This task assumes the difficulty assignment (H2) of the 'high school Basic Math 1 track' and does not indicate in which grade the content is learned (school arrangements vary). Middle school level solving of linear equations and the fact that 'you cannot divide by 0.'
y-m-54-02.s.s1.prompt: You want to say the solution of this equation as a single value without knowing the values of a and b. Pick the most appropriate thing you need to know more.
y-m-54-02.s.s1.hint.0: Put in values like 3 and 2 for a one at a time and write how the equation changes.
y-m-54-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether there is a need for a condition on the number when you divide both sides by the same number.
y-m-54-02.s.s1.o.a: It is enough to know only whether b is 3
y-m-54-02.s.s1.r.a: If you set b=3 the right side becomes 0, but the conclusion changes again depending on whether the coefficient on the left is 0.
y-m-54-02.s.s1.o.b: We need to know whether a-2 is 0 or not
y-m-54-02.s.s1.r.b: You are seeing that the condition on the number you divide by can split the conclusion.
y-m-54-02.s.s1.o.c: It is enough to know only that a and b are both integers
y-m-54-02.s.s1.r.c: The property of being an integer does not affect the number of solutions. When a=2, it is also an integer.
y-m-54-02.s.s1.o.d: It is enough to know only whether x is positive
y-m-54-02.s.s1.r.d: Knowing the sign of x is far from the information that splits the number of solutions. Look at the coefficient side.
y-m-54-02.s.s1.explain: If the coefficient a-2 of x is not 0, you can divide and there is one solution. If a-2=0, the equation becomes 0·x=b-3, and when b-3 is 0 there are infinitely many solutions, and otherwise there is no solution. So you need to know whether a-2 is 0.
y-m-54-02.s.s2.prompt: Decide integers a and b so that the equation (a-2)x = b-3 has no solution at all, and enter 2 different examples. (a and b are integers from -20 to 20)
y-m-54-02.s.s2.hint.0: Put 2 in for a to make the left side simple, and look at whether it gives the same value for any x you put in.
y-m-54-02.s.s2.hint.1: Split into the case where the right side b-3 is 0 and the case where it is not 0, and put in one value of x directly.
y-m-54-02.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are integers within the range.
y-m-54-02.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers from -20 to 20.
y-m-54-02.s.s2.fail.c2: If the coefficient a-2 of x is not 0, there is one solution.
y-m-54-02.s.s2.ok.c3: 0·x equals a nonzero number, so there is no solution.
y-m-54-02.s.s2.fail.c3: If the right side is 0, there are infinitely many solutions. Try to make the right side a nonzero number.
y-m-54-02.s.s2.explain: If a=2, the left side is 0·x=0, so when the right side b-3 is a nonzero number, no x you put in works, so there is no solution. If b=3, every x is a solution. If a is not 2, there is exactly one solution.
y-m-54-02.s.s3.prompt: Write the answer to send to Harin. Write in which case Harin's 'there is always one solution' does not hold and what happens to the solution in that case.
y-m-54-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write what value the 'number you divide by' in Harin's calculation can take.
y-m-54-02.s.s3.hint.1: Find the a that makes that value 0 and write what form the equation takes then.
y-m-54-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write by splitting into the case a=2 and the case where it is not?
y-m-54-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you reflect that when a=2 the result differs depending on whether b-3 is 0 or not?
y-m-54-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did your explanation point out that Harin's solution (dividing) is not wrong but 'the check of the condition was missing'?
y-m-54-02.s.s3.model.0: If a is 2, then a-2 is 0, so you cannot divide both sides by it. Then it becomes 0·x=b-3, so if b is not 3 there is no solution, and if b is 3 every x is a solution. Only when a is not 2 is there one solution, x=(b-3)/(a-2).
y-m-54-02.s.s3.model.1: Before dividing, we have to check whether a=2. If a=2 you would be dividing by 0, which is not allowed, and then if b=3 there are infinitely many solutions and if b is not 3 there is no solution. If a is not 2, there is one solution just as Harin said.
y-m-54-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: Only the order of splitting into cases is different, and the content is the same.

y-m-54-03.title: If we change k, how do the solutions change?
y-m-54-03.topic: The number of real roots of the quadratic equation x²-4x+k=0, and the k that give integer roots
y-m-54-03.goal: See how the number of real roots of a quadratic equation containing the letter k changes with k, make k values that give two different integer roots yourself, and explain the rule.
y-m-54-03.material: In the equation x²-4x+k=0, k is an integer, and the solutions are considered among the real numbers. If you change k, the number and form of the solutions change. Subin decided to find the solutions while changing k to 0, 3, 4, 5, -1. x²-4x+k is read as 'x squared minus 4x plus k.'
y-m-54-03.thinking.0: Putting values in for k and comparing the number of roots
y-m-54-03.thinking.1: Making several examples that fit the conditions
y-m-54-03.thinking.2: Explaining the rule in the examples found
y-m-54-03.prereq.0: This task assumes the difficulty assignment (H2) of the 'high school Basic Math 1 track' and does not indicate in which grade the content is learned (school arrangements vary). Middle school level solving of quadratic equations (factoring, the quadratic formula) and the meaning of square numbers (1, 4, 9, 16, ...).
y-m-54-03.s.s1.prompt: Pick all the k for which there are two different real solutions. (k is the constant term of the equation above)
y-m-54-03.s.s1.hint.0: Put in the k one at a time and rewrite the equation in the form (x-2)² = (some number).
y-m-54-03.s.s1.hint.1: Work out how many solutions there are when the number on the right is positive, 0, and negative.
y-m-54-03.s.s1.r.a: This is an approach that checks by solving directly whether two different solutions come out.
y-m-54-03.s.s1.r.b: You may have counted the case with only one solution (a repeated solution) as two different solutions. Try factoring x²-4x+4.
y-m-54-03.s.s1.r.c: You may have thought that the larger k is, the more solutions there are. In the equation x²-4x+5=0, look at what value (x-2)² would have to be.
y-m-54-03.s.s1.r.d: This is an approach that checks by solving directly whether two different solutions come out.
y-m-54-03.s.s1.r.e: You did not miss the fact that a negative k can also have solutions.
y-m-54-03.s.s1.explain: Since x²-4x+k=(x-2)²+k-4, we get (x-2)²=4-k. If 4-k>0, that is k<4, there are two different solutions; if k=4 there is one solution; and if k>4 there are no real solutions.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 integers k for which x²-4x+k=0 has two different integers as its solutions. (k is an integer -60 or more, and the solutions are two different integers among the real numbers)
y-m-54-03.s.s2.hint.0: Look at the coefficients of x²-4x and think about what the sum of the two solutions must be.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.hint.1: Pick two integers with that sum, take them as the two solutions, and calculate what k becomes.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.ok.c1: k is an integer -60 or more.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.fail.c1: k must be an integer -60 or more.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.ok.c2: This is the range where there are two different real solutions.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.fail.c2: If k is 4 or more, two different solutions do not come out.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The two solutions come out as exact integers.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The solutions are not integers. Find the form of the solutions directly and check.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.explain: If k=0, the solutions are 0, 4. If k=3, 1, 3. If k=-5, -1, 5. If k=-12, -2, 6. In all of them the sum of the solutions is 4 and the product is k. For the integers k=1, 2, the solutions are not integers.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.because.prompt: What rule do the k you found follow? Also write, with at least one numerical example, why k=1 or k=2 does not work.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the two solutions found for k=0, 3, -5 side by side and compare the sum and product of the two solutions.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check whether the solutions of x²-4x+1=0, made when k=1, are integers.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g. The sum of the two solutions is ...
y-m-54-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does the rule I gave explain all 3 examples in s2?
y-m-54-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Can the rule screen out cases that do not work, like k=1?
y-m-54-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you use the rule to predict one more new k and check it?
y-m-54-03.s.s2.because.model.0: The sum of the two solutions must always be 4. If you pick two integers with sum 4, k becomes their product. For example, with 1 and 3, k=3, and with -1 and 5, k=-5. If k=1, the product is 1, and there are no integers with sum 4.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.because.model.1: 16-4k must be a square number greater than 0 for the roots to come out as integers. For k=3 it is 4, for k=0 it is 16, and for k=-5 it is 36, all square numbers. For k=1 it is 12, which is not a square number, so it does not work.
y-m-54-03.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: This is another method that explains by whether the calculated value is a square number instead of the sum and product.

y-m-54-04.title: Why is one of the two values not a solution?
y-m-54-04.topic: Checking the values obtained when solving an equation with absolute values
y-m-54-04.goal: Find where the assumption 'every value that comes out of solving is a solution' breaks in the solution of |x-1|=2x, and explain in your own way why only one solution remains.
y-m-54-04.material: Seoa solved the equation |x-1| = 2x. x is a real number. |x-1| is read as 'the absolute value of x minus 1.' Seoa's solution is below.
y-m-54-04.thinking.0: Checking the last line of the solution
y-m-54-04.thinking.2: Showing the same conclusion by another method
y-m-54-04.prereq.0: This task assumes the difficulty assignment (H2) of the 'high school Basic Math 1 track' and does not indicate in which grade the content is learned (school arrangements vary). The meaning of absolute value (the distance from 0 on the number line, always 0 or more) and middle school level solving of linear equations.
y-m-54-04.s.s1.prompt: Pick one wrong line in Seoa's solution. (Lines are counted from 1.)
y-m-54-04.s.s1.hint.0: Solve lines 1 to 3 again to check each calculation, and then look at what new claim is made in the lines after that.
y-m-54-04.s.s1.hint.1: Substitute the two values one at a time into the original equation |x-1|=2x and calculate both sides.
y-m-54-04.s.s1.line.3: Therefore the solutions are x=-1 or x=1/3.
y-m-54-04.s.s1.line.4: These are the two values obtained by solving, so both are solutions of this equation.
y-m-54-04.s.s1.explain: Lines 4 and 5. In the process of solving, there is no guarantee that the solutions of the expressions from the split cases are solutions of the original equation. If you put x=-1 into the original equation, the left side is |-2|=2 and the right side is 2×(-1)=-2, which differ. For x=1/3, the left side is 2/3 and the right side is 2/3, which match.
y-m-54-04.s.s2.prompt: If you put x=-1 into the original equation, the left side is |-1-1|=2 and the right side is 2×(-1)=-2. Pick the most appropriate thing to say from this result.
y-m-54-04.s.s2.hint.0: Think about what the smallest value the left side |x-1| can have is.
y-m-54-04.s.s2.hint.1: Work out whether the equation can hold in the range of x where the right side 2x is negative.
y-m-54-04.s.s2.o.a: |x-1| is 0 or more but 2x is negative, so it does not fit
y-m-54-04.s.s2.r.a: This is thinking that first looks at the range of values one side of the equation can have.
y-m-54-04.s.s2.o.b: Because of the absolute value, numbers with different signs can be seen as the same number, so this is a solution too
y-m-54-04.s.s2.r.b: The absolute value erases the sign only on the left side. It has no effect on the right side 2x.
y-m-54-04.s.s2.o.c: There was a calculation mistake, and if you solve it again both values are solutions
y-m-54-04.s.s2.r.c: If you call it an error even though the substituted calculation is right, you may not be trusting the result you checked.
y-m-54-04.s.s2.o.d: x=-1 is a solution and x=1/3 is not a solution
y-m-54-04.s.s2.r.d: You may have picked just one in order without substituting both values to check. Substitute 1/3 as well.
y-m-54-04.s.s2.explain: |x-1| is always 0 or more, so 2x must also be 0 or more. For x=-1, 2x is negative, so it does not fit, and for x=1/3 both sides are 2/3. So the only solution is x=1/3.
y-m-54-04.s.s3.prompt: Instead of Seoa's method, write one other method that shows that x=1/3 is the only solution. For example: decide the range of x first, or split into x≥1 and x<1. Also write why x=-1 is not a solution.
y-m-54-04.s.s3.hint.0: Put x=-1 into both sides of the original equation and compare the signs.
y-m-54-04.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what values an absolute value can be at least, and write what condition is attached to the expression on the right.
y-m-54-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Can you explain where my method puts the 'reason for filtering out the solution' differently from Seoa's method?
y-m-54-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check by putting it into the original equation that x=1/3 really is a solution?
y-m-54-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is the reason for discarding x=-1 clear, either by the range or by substitution?
y-m-54-04.s.s3.model.0: |x-1| is 0 or more, so 2x must be 0 or more, so x≥0. Then x=-1 is discarded and only x=1/3 remains. If you put in 1/3, both sides are equal to 2/3.
y-m-54-04.s.s3.model.1: When x≥1, x-1=2x gives x=-1, but that is not x≥1, so it does not work. When x<1, 1-x=2x gives x=1/3, which satisfies x<1. So the only solution is x=1/3.
y-m-54-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: It reached the same conclusion by the method of splitting the range.

y-m-54-05.title: Is it OK to multiply both sides by x?
y-m-54-05.topic: A condition to check before multiplying by a variable in a fractional inequality
y-m-54-05.goal: Build a counterexample yourself to the conclusion x<3 obtained by multiplying both sides of 6/x>2 by x, and rewrite the solution to reflect that the direction of the inequality sign depends on the sign of x.
y-m-54-05.material: Jiho wrote this while solving the inequality 6/x > 2 (x is a nonzero real number). “If I multiply both sides by x, 6 > 2x, so x < 3. So x=-1 is a solution too.” 6/x is read as '6 over x.'
y-m-54-05.thinking.0: Choosing examples to test the claim
y-m-54-05.thinking.2: Splitting the conditions and correcting the conclusion
y-m-54-05.prereq.0: This task assumes the difficulty assignment (H2) of the 'high school Basic Math 1 track' and does not indicate in which grade the content is learned (school arrangements vary). Middle school level linear inequalities (multiplying by a negative number reverses the inequality sign) and calculating values of fractional expressions.
y-m-54-05.s.s1.prompt: We want to check whether Jiho's conclusion 'if x<3 then 6/x>2' is right. Pick the appropriate first thing to do.
y-m-54-05.s.s1.hint.0: Split the values with x<3 into positive and negative, and pick two or three of each.
y-m-54-05.s.s1.hint.1: Put each value into 6/x and organize in a table whether it is greater or less than 2.
y-m-54-05.s.s1.o.a: Multiply both sides by 2 and see whether the expressions become equal
y-m-54-05.s.s1.r.a: A new expression made by multiplying both sides by the same number is not directly related to whether the original conclusion is right or wrong.
y-m-54-05.s.s1.o.b: Substitute x=3 and see whether the two sides are equal
y-m-54-05.s.s1.r.b: Checking only the boundary value does not test the whole of x<3.
y-m-54-05.s.s1.o.c: Divide 6/x by x to simplify the expression
y-m-54-05.s.s1.r.c: That only makes the expression more complicated and is not an action that tests the conclusion.
y-m-54-05.s.s1.o.d: Substitute a few values with x<3 into the original inequality
y-m-54-05.s.s1.r.d: This is an approach that directly tests some of the cases the conclusion talks about.
y-m-54-05.s.s1.explain: The claim 'if x<3 it always holds' is broken if even one value with x<3 does not make the inequality hold. Directly substituting into the original inequality 6/x>2 is the most direct way.
y-m-54-05.s.s2.prompt: Enter 2 different integers x for which Jiho's conclusion x<3 holds but the original inequality 6/x>2 does not hold. (x is an integer from -50 to 50, and x is not 0)
y-m-54-05.s.s2.hint.0: Put one negative and one positive integer with x<3 into 6/x.
y-m-54-05.s.s2.hint.1: Look at whether 6/x is greater than 2 together with its sign.
y-m-54-05.s.s2.ok.c1: x is an integer within the range, not 0.
y-m-54-05.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be a nonzero integer from -50 to 50.
y-m-54-05.s.s2.ok.c3: 6/x is 2 or less, so the original inequality does not hold.
y-m-54-05.s.s2.fail.c3: 6/x is greater than 2, so the original inequality holds. It is not a counterexample.
y-m-54-05.s.s2.explain: If x=-1, then 6/x=-6, and -6 is not greater than 2. Even with x<3 there are values for which it does not hold, so Jiho's conclusion is not right. These values are all negative.
y-m-54-05.s.s3.prompt: Fix Jiho's solution. Write together where the problem was and the range of the solution obtained correctly.
y-m-54-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write separately the expression you get by multiplying both sides by x when x is positive and when x is negative.
y-m-54-05.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether x=-1 is included when you combine the results of the two cases.
y-m-54-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you think by splitting into the case where x is positive and the case where x is negative?
y-m-54-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you decide the direction of the inequality sign separately in each case?
y-m-54-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check that the range of your solution does not include x=-1, which Jiho got wrong?
y-m-54-05.s.s3.model.0: The problem is that you multiplied by x without knowing the sign of x. If x is negative, the direction of the inequality sign reverses. Only when x>0 does it become 6>2x, so the solution is 0<x<3.
y-m-54-05.s.s3.model.1: If x>0, then 6>2x, so 0<x<3. If x<0, the inequality sign reverses to 6<2x, that is x>3, but that does not overlap with x<0, so there is no solution. So the solution is 0<x<3.
y-m-54-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: It also calculated the negative case separately and showed that there is no solution.

y-m-54-06.title: When we multiply square roots, can we just multiply the numbers inside?
y-m-54-06.topic: The condition for using √a·√b=√(ab) in multiplication that includes square roots of negative numbers
y-m-54-06.goal: Find the line that goes wrong in a solution that wrote √(-2)·√(-3) as √6, and check the cases where the rule √a·√b=√(ab) holds with examples you make yourself.
y-m-54-06.material: The imaginary unit i satisfies i²=-1, and we agree that for a positive number c, √(-c)=i√c. Daeun wrote a solution that calculates √(-2)·√(-3) as below. √(-2) is read as 'the square root of negative 2.'
y-m-54-06.thinking.0: Checking the condition under which the rule is used
y-m-54-06.thinking.1: Comparing two solving methods to resolve the contradiction
y-m-54-06.prereq.0: This task assumes the difficulty assignment (H2) of the 'high school Basic Math 1 track' and does not indicate in which grade the content is learned (school arrangements vary). The imaginary unit i (i²=-1), the agreement that √(-a)=i√a for a positive number a, and √a·√b=√(ab) for positive numbers.
y-m-54-06.s.s1.prompt: Pick one line in Daeun's solution whose reasoning is not right. (Lines are counted from 1.)
y-m-54-06.s.s1.hint.0: The same product √(-2)·√(-3) came out as different values in line 2 and line 3. Compare how the calculation methods of the two lines differ.
y-m-54-06.s.s1.hint.1: Recall what condition there was for the product of two positive numbers, √2·√3=√6.
y-m-54-06.s.s1.line.2: On the other hand, i√2 · i√3 = i²·√6 = -√6.
y-m-54-06.s.s1.explain: Line 2. √a·√b=√(ab) cannot be used when a and b are both negative. If you change to i first and then calculate, as in lines 1 and 3, √(-2)·√(-3) = -√6. The contradiction in line 4 happens because the rule was used wrongly in line 2.
y-m-54-06.s.s2.prompt: Pick the most accurate description of the cases where √a·√b=√(ab) holds. (a and b are real numbers, and square roots of negative numbers are handled by the agreement above)
y-m-54-06.s.s2.hint.0: Using i, calculate both sides for the four pairs (-4, 9), (4, 9), (-4, -9), (0, -5) and compare them in a table.
y-m-54-06.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the sign pattern of the pairs that gave the same value with the sign pattern of the pair that came out different.
y-m-54-06.s.s2.o.a: It always holds as long as a and b are integers
y-m-54-06.s.s2.r.a: Being an integer has nothing to do with the agreement on square roots of negative numbers. (-2) and (-3) are integers too.
y-m-54-06.s.s2.o.b: It does not hold if either a or b is negative
y-m-54-06.s.s2.r.b: Even when there is only one negative number, if you calculate directly, the same value can come out. Check with (-4) and 9.
y-m-54-06.s.s2.o.c: It holds only when a and b are both positive
y-m-54-06.s.s2.r.c: You took the cases where it holds narrowly, as only some of them. It is a safe condition, but it is not the exact boundary.
y-m-54-06.s.s2.o.d: It holds unless a and b are both negative
y-m-54-06.s.s2.r.d: You calculated a few examples and found the pattern of the cases that do not hold.
y-m-54-06.s.s2.explain: If one of a and b is negative and the other is 0 or more, it holds (for example √(-4)·√9=6i=√(-36)), and it fails only when both are negative. Taking it that it holds only when both are positive is safe but is an overly narrow condition.
y-m-54-06.s.s2.acc.0: If both are positive it always holds, so it is a safe condition, but there are cases where it holds even when only one number is negative, so it is not the exact condition.
y-m-54-06.s.s3.prompt: Enter 3 different integer pairs (a, b) in which at least one of a and b is negative and yet √a·√b=√(ab) holds. (a and b are integers from -50 to 50, and pairs with the order swapped count as the same example)
y-m-54-06.s.s3.hint.0: Pick a pair like (-4, 9) and, using i, calculate both sides separately.
y-m-54-06.s.s3.hint.1: For a pair you made yourself in the same way, calculate both sides and check whether they are equal.
y-m-54-06.s.s3.ok.c1: a and b are integers within the range.
y-m-54-06.s.s3.fail.c1: a and b must be integers from -50 to 50.
y-m-54-06.s.s3.ok.c2: At least one of them is negative.
y-m-54-06.s.s3.fail.c2: Both are 0 or more. There must be at least one negative number.
y-m-54-06.s.s3.ok.c3: They are not both negative (that case does not hold).
y-m-54-06.s.s3.fail.c3: Both are negative. The rule does not hold in this case.
y-m-54-06.s.s3.explain: If one number is negative and the other is 0 or more, √a·√b=√(ab) holds. For example: (-4,9) → 2i·3=6i, √(-36)=6i. (0,-5) → 0 and 0. A pair where both are negative does not match.

y-m-54-07.title: There is one equation, so is there one answer?
y-m-54-07.topic: How count and condition information changes the number of solutions in a problem with only one equation
y-m-54-07.goal: Check step by step that even with only one equation, conditions like 'a whole number 0 or more' and 'at least 1 of each' can reduce the number of solutions, then change the conditions and find all the possible combinations yourself.
y-m-54-07.material: At a stationery store, candy costs 800원 each and chocolate costs 500원 each. A student bought x candies and y chocolates and paid a total of 7000원. x and y are integers (counts) 0 or more. Let's follow how your thinking changes each time you learn one piece of information.
y-m-54-07.thinking.0: Following how the possible cases change as information increases
y-m-54-07.thinking.1: Checking whether new information conflicts with earlier judgments
y-m-54-07.thinking.2: Finding all the possible combinations under the conditions
y-m-54-07.prereq.0: This task assumes the difficulty assignment (H2) of the 'high school Basic Math 1 track' and does not indicate in which grade the content is learned (school arrangements vary). Middle school level linear expressions, the concepts of natural numbers and integers, and calculating a total with multiplication and addition.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.prompt: Read the information one piece at a time and choose a prediction about the possible (number of candies, number of chocolates). You may keep or change the prediction you chose earlier.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.hint.0: Write the possible values of x starting from 0 and check one by one whether y is an integer in the second line.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.hint.1: When new information comes in, cross out and check which combinations remain from the list you made earlier.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.0.info: What you know: only the fact that 800×x + 500×y = 7000. You do not know the numbers of candies and chocolates individually.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think about the possible (x, y) combinations?
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.0.after: If x=0, then y=14, and if x=5, then y=6. x=10 makes y=-2, which cannot be a count, and if x is not a multiple of 5, like x=1 to 4, y is not an integer. Therefore only two combinations, (0,14) and (5,6), are possible. 'd' is a judgment put off by looking only at the information, so the difference is that if you work it out, you can say more.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: There is only one equation, so there are infinitely many combinations
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You may have forgotten the condition that x and y are integers 0 or more. If x=1, work out whether y is an integer.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Counts are integers 0 or more, so the possible combinations are limited to a few, and we can work them out directly
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This prediction shows the thinking of trying to work out the possible cases based on the information known so far.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is decided to be exactly one
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: There are two unknowns in one equation, but you treated it as decided to be one right away. Work out what y is when x=0.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.0.o.d: There is not enough information to say anything
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You put off the judgment before working out a few directly. If you work it out, you can say the number of combinations.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.1.info: Newly learned: This student bought at least 1 candy and at least 1 chocolate.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: What do you think about the possible combinations now?
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.1.after: (0,14), with 0 candies, does not fit 'at least 1 of each,' so it drops out and only (5,6) remains. There is still one equation, but the conditions 'whole-number counts' and 'at least 1' made the answer a single one.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Even after reading 'at least 1 of each,' you kept the combination with 0 candies.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: A condition was added, yet you thought it increased. A condition works in the direction of reducing the possible cases.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This prediction shows the thinking of trying to work out the possible cases based on the information known so far.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It is still not decided, so one more condition is needed
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You may not have checked the list of combinations from the previous step against the new condition.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.2.info: One more piece of information: the store clerk remembered, “There were more candies than chocolates.”
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: How do you see this information in relation to your judgment so far, and what will you do?
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.2.after: In (5,6), there are fewer than 6 candies. (6,5) gives 800×6+500×5=7300, so the total does not match. Therefore the calculation and the clerk's memory conflict, and it is reasonable either to recheck the unit prices, total, and 'at least 1,' or to doubt the clerk's memory. Which one to trust depends on additional evidence (such as a receipt).
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.2.o.a: In (5,6) there are fewer candies, so it conflicts with what the clerk said. Recheck the total, unit prices, and conditions, or doubt the clerk's memory
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This prediction shows the thinking of trying to work out the possible cases based on the information known so far.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Change to (6,5) to fit what the clerk said
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Put (6,5) into the total. You did not check whether 800×6+500×5 is 7000.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Even if they conflict, keep (5,6) obtained by calculation as it is, and leave open the possibility that the clerk's memory is wrong
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This prediction shows the thinking of trying to work out the possible cases based on the information known so far.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Just pick either one of the two pieces of information
y-m-54-07.s.s1.st.2.r.d: If you pick without a reason, there is no reason you changed your judgment.
y-m-54-07.s.s1.reflect: If you write down the possible cases as a list each time new information comes in, you can say why your judgment changes (whether a condition reduced the cases or the pieces of information conflict with each other).
y-m-54-07.s.s2.prompt: At the same store, a notebook costs 300원 each and a pencil costs 500원 each. The total is 4200원, and you bought at least 1 of each, x notebooks and y pencils. Enter 2 different possible (x, y). (x and y are integers)
y-m-54-07.s.s2.hint.0: Increase the number of pencils y starting from 1 and check whether the remaining amount is divisible by the price of a notebook.
y-m-54-07.s.s2.hint.1: Look back and check whether the combination you found is right by calculating 3×(number of notebooks)+5×(number of pencils).
y-m-54-07.s.s2.ok.c1: x and y are integers 1 or more.
y-m-54-07.s.s2.fail.c1: x and y must be integers 1 or more.
y-m-54-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The total does not come to 4200원. Multiply and add it up directly.
y-m-54-07.s.s2.explain: From 3x+5y=42, x=4, y=6 or x=9, y=3. x=14, y=0 has 0 pencils, so it does not fit the conditions. This time, even with all the conditions kept, two cases are possible, so unlike the earlier case where the conditions made it one, additional information is needed.

y-m-54-08.title: If three examples are right, is it always so?
y-m-54-08.topic: Whether the product of irrational numbers can be rational
y-m-54-08.goal: Learn that the claim 'the product of irrational numbers is always irrational' is not guaranteed by a few examples, then make pairs of irrational numbers whose product is rational yourself and rewrite the claim.
y-m-54-08.material: Hayun said, “If you multiply two irrational numbers, it's always irrational. √2×√3=√6, √2×√5=√10, √3×√5=√15 are all irrational, aren't they?” In this task, √p is regarded as irrational when p is a positive integer that is not a square number. √2 is read as 'root 2.'
y-m-54-08.thinking.0: Telling apart a few examples from a general claim
y-m-54-08.prereq.0: This task assumes the difficulty assignment (H2) of the 'high school Basic Math 1 track' and does not indicate in which grade the content is learned (school arrangements vary). Distinguishing irrational and rational numbers (the positive square root of an integer that is not a square number is irrational), and √a·√b=√(ab) (a, b positive).
y-m-54-08.s.s1.prompt: Pick the most appropriate judgment about Hayun's evidence and conclusion.
y-m-54-08.s.s1.hint.0: Change the number multiplied with √2 to a form other than √3 and √5.
y-m-54-08.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate what happens if the result of the product comes to fall inside a square number.
y-m-54-08.s.s1.o.a: All three examples are right, so we can consider that it always holds
y-m-54-08.s.s1.r.a: You are treating the fact that several examples are right as a proof of the general rule.
y-m-54-08.s.s1.o.b: We should consider that the product of irrational numbers is always rational
y-m-54-08.s.s1.r.b: You generalized in the opposite way from the results of a few examples. In those same examples, the products were irrational.
y-m-54-08.s.s1.o.c: Even if the examples are right, 'always' is not guaranteed, so we look for a counterexample
y-m-54-08.s.s1.r.c: You are seeing that the number of examples shown and the scope of the claim are different.
y-m-54-08.s.s1.o.d: We should judge by changing it from a product to a sum
y-m-54-08.s.s1.r.d: You changed the operation in the question. You can test the product itself.
y-m-54-08.s.s1.explain: The claim 'always' can be broken by a single example, so collecting right examples does not guarantee it. Finding an example where the product is rational is the direct test.
y-m-54-08.s.s2.prompt: Enter 3 different pairs of integers p, q such that the product of the two irrational numbers √p and √q is rational. Conditions: p and q are different integers from 2 to 100, and neither p nor q is a square number. (Pairs with the order swapped count as the same example.)
y-m-54-08.s.s2.hint.0: Think of the number that becomes a square number when multiplied with √2 in the form 2×(some number).
y-m-54-08.s.s2.hint.1: For the pairs you found, calculate p×q and check whether it is the square of some number.
y-m-54-08.s.s2.ok.c1: p and q are integers within the range.
y-m-54-08.s.s2.fail.c1: p and q must be integers from 2 to 100.
y-m-54-08.s.s2.ok.c2: p and q are different from each other.
y-m-54-08.s.s2.fail.c2: p and q are the same. They must be different numbers.
y-m-54-08.s.s2.fail.c3: One of the two is a square number, so it is rational. Both must be irrational.
y-m-54-08.s.s2.ok.c4: The product pq is a square number, so √p·√q is rational.
y-m-54-08.s.s2.fail.c4: The product pq is not a square number, so √p·√q is irrational.
y-m-54-08.s.s2.explain: The product becomes rational, as in √2×√8=√16=4, √3×√12=√36=6, √5×√20=√100=10. If you make p and q both a square-number multiple of one number, the product becomes a square number and so it works out that way.
y-m-54-08.s.s3.prompt: Write the answer to send to Hayun. Using an example you made yourself, write what is wrong with Hayun's claim and how it should be said if corrected.
y-m-54-08.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one pair you made above and calculate √p×√q by combining it under one radical sign.
y-m-54-08.s.s3.hint.1: Put that result side by side with Hayun's sentence 'always irrational' and compare.
y-m-54-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In the example I gave, is it clear that both numbers are irrational and the product is rational?
y-m-54-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does the corrected claim state the scope exactly, like 'sometimes irrational and sometimes rational'?
y-m-54-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you point out that Hayun's three examples were not wrong but that 'the generalization went too far'?
y-m-54-08.s.s3.model.0: The product can be rational, as in √2×√8=√16=4. So 'irrational times irrational is always irrational' is wrong. We should say that the product is sometimes irrational and sometimes rational.
y-m-54-08.s.s3.model.1: √3×√12=√36=6. 6 is rational, so it is a counterexample. The three examples Hayun saw just happened to be irrational, and a few examples cannot guarantee 'always.'
y-m-54-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: It pointed out both the counterexample and the limit of generalization.

y-m-54-09.title: How far can we go with only the values in a table?
y-m-54-09.topic: Guessing the solutions of the inequalities f(x)<0 and f(x)≤0 from a table and conditions of a quadratic function
y-m-54-09.goal: When there is only a table of function values, tell apart what can be said for certain about where f(x)<0, and follow how the solution gets decided as information increases and how the difference between < and ≤ shows up in the solution.
y-m-54-09.material: There is a quadratic function f(x). The coefficient of x² in f(x) is positive, so the graph is U-shaped. The values of f(x) are revealed step by step. f(-2) is read as 'f of negative 2.'
y-m-54-09.thinking.0: Telling apart what is certain and what is a guess
y-m-54-09.thinking.1: Updating a judgment with new information
y-m-54-09.thinking.2: Checking the wrong line of a solution
y-m-54-09.prereq.0: This task assumes the difficulty assignment (H2) of the 'high school Basic Math 1 track' and does not indicate in which grade the content is learned (school arrangements vary). The shape of the quadratic function y=ax²+bx+c (U-shaped if a>0), calculating function values, and the basics of factoring.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.prompt: Read the known information and choose a prediction about the x that satisfy f(x)<0. You may keep or change the earlier prediction.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.hint.0: Mark whether each value in the table is positive, 0, or negative, and imagine where the U shape rises upward.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.hint.1: Each time new information comes in, check again whether what you said was certain before is still right.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.0.info: What you know: f(-2)=5, f(0)=-3, f(4)=5.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: What can you say for certain now about the x that satisfy f(x)<0?
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.0.after: f(0)=-3<0, so x=0 is certainly included. The shape is a U and f(-2) and f(4) are positive, so the x with f(x)<0 can only be between -2 and 4. But we do not yet know the exact boundaries. 'c' and 'd' are both different facts that can be said for certain now.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The only x that satisfies f(x)<0 is 0
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You treated only the points where the value was checked as solutions. We do not yet know the values between points, but we can use the U shape.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You concluded that everything inside is negative just by seeing that the end values are positive. We do not yet know the values between 0 and -2.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This prediction shows the thinking of trying to work out the possible cases based on the information known so far.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.0.o.d: If there are x that satisfy f(x)<0, they are all between -2 and 4
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is thinking that uses the U shape and the signs of the end values together.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: What do you think about the range of x that satisfies f(x)<0?
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.1.after: In the U shape, f is 0 at -1 and 3, so it is negative between them and positive outside. f(x)<0 means 'less than 0,' so the boundaries -1 and 3 are not included, giving -1<x<3. It does not conflict with x=0, which you said was certain in the earlier step, being inside this range.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You looked at the negative interval and the positive interval of the U shape the other way around. Check whether it fits f(0)=-3.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Even though you saw that f is 0 at the boundaries -1 and 3, you put them in under the condition 'less than 0.'
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You treated only the points where f is 0 as solutions. These points are not values less than 0.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This prediction shows the thinking of trying to work out the possible cases based on the information known so far.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.2.info: The condition has changed. This function is f(x)=x²-2x-3. (You can check by calculating directly that it fits every value in the table.) Now the question is the range of x where f(x)≤0, that is, 'is 0 or less.'
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: What do you think about the range of x that satisfies f(x)≤0?
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.2.after: f(-1)=0 and f(3)=0 are also 0 or less, so the boundaries are included, giving -1≤x≤3. When the inequality sign changes from < to ≤, the boundary values enter the solution.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You did not reflect that ≤ includes 'equal.' Look at what f(-1) and f(3) are.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Seeing ≤, you changed it to the outside intervals. Check whether f(0)=-3 is 0 or less.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This prediction shows the thinking of trying to work out the possible cases based on the information known so far.
y-m-54-09.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You treated only the confirmed point as a solution. Are the values inside also all 0 or less?
y-m-54-09.s.s1.reflect: From a few values in a table, you can tell apart 'what is certain (the sign of function values, the range obtained from the U shape)' and 'what is still unknown (the exact boundaries),' and as information increases, the certain range narrows.
y-m-54-09.s.s2.prompt: This is Seungu's solution that found the solution of f(x)<0 when f(x)=x²-2x-3. Pick one wrong line. (Lines are counted from 1.)
y-m-54-09.s.s2.hint.0: Put x=-3 into the result of line 4, x<3, and calculate whether the original inequality f(x)<0 holds.
y-m-54-09.s.s2.hint.1: Organize in a table which sign combinations make the product negative.
y-m-54-09.s.s2.line.2: The product is negative, so x+1<0 or x-3<0.
y-m-54-09.s.s2.line.3: Therefore x<-1 or x<3, that is, x<3.
y-m-54-09.s.s2.explain: Line 3 (and line 4, which results from it) is the problem. For the product to be negative, the signs of the two factors must be different. If you say 'at least one of them is negative,' it includes the case where both factors are negative, and then the product is positive. For example, if x=-3, then (-2)(-6)=12, which is positive. The correct answer is -1<x<3. (Choosing either line 3 or line 4 is accepted as correct.)

y-m-54-10.title: If it works at x=1, is the expression right?
y-m-54-10.topic: A solution that decided the coefficients by substituting one value, and the condition for holding at every x
y-m-54-10.goal: Learn why checking one value is not enough in a solution that decides a and b so that ax+b=3x-2 holds for every x, then make other (a, b) that satisfy that same one condition and explain it to a friend.
y-m-54-10.material: Seojin is solving the problem “Decide a and b so that ax+b=3x-2 always holds (for every x), regardless of x.” Seojin put in x=1 to get a+b=1, decided (a, b)=(1, 0), and said, “At x=1 both sides are equal to 1, so the answer is right.” ax+b is read as 'a times x plus b.'
y-m-54-10.thinking.0: Judging whether the check is enough
y-m-54-10.thinking.1: Making examples that satisfy only one condition
y-m-54-10.thinking.2: Explaining in a way suited to a friend
y-m-54-10.prereq.0: This task assumes the difficulty assignment (H2) of the 'high school Basic Math 1 track' and does not indicate in which grade the content is learned (school arrangements vary). Calculating values of linear expressions, substituting into a linear expression with two unknowns, and the meaning of 'it holds for every x.'
y-m-54-10.s.s1.prompt: Pick the most appropriate judgment about Seojin's check, 'when (a, b)=(1, 0), both sides are equal at x=1.'
y-m-54-10.s.s1.hint.0: Put the (a, b)=(1, 0) that Seojin decided into ax+b and calculate the value at another x.
y-m-54-10.s.s1.hint.1: In the same way, write the value of 3x-2 beside it and compare.
y-m-54-10.s.s1.o.a: Both sides are equal, so it is confirmed that it holds for every x
y-m-54-10.s.s1.r.a: You generalized a value being right at one place to all cases.
y-m-54-10.s.s1.o.b: We cannot know yet. We need to check whether it holds at other x too
y-m-54-10.s.s1.r.b: You are seeing that the scope of the check is narrower than 'every x.'
y-m-54-10.s.s1.o.c: If there is just the one condition a+b=1, it holds for every x
y-m-54-10.s.s1.r.c: You treated the one condition a+b=1 as replacing the conditions for every x.
y-m-54-10.s.s1.o.d: You cannot check by putting values in for x; you have to compare the coefficients
y-m-54-10.s.s1.r.d: You can check by substitution. Calculate both sides at x=2.
y-m-54-10.s.s1.explain: Being equal at x=1 only confirms the one condition a+b=1. At x=2, (1, 0) gives 2 on the left and 4 on the right, which differ, so it does not hold for every x.
y-m-54-10.s.s2.prompt: Like Seojin's, enter 3 different (a, b) for which both sides are equal at x=1 but it does not hold for every x. (a and b are integers from -20 to 20)
y-m-54-10.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a value for a and decide b so that a+b=1.
y-m-54-10.s.s2.hint.1: With the (a, b) you picked, calculate whether both sides are equal at an x other than x=1.
y-m-54-10.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are integers within the range.
y-m-54-10.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers from -20 to 20.
y-m-54-10.s.s2.ok.c2: Both sides are equal at x=1.
y-m-54-10.s.s2.fail.c2: Both sides are not equal when x=1 is put in.
y-m-54-10.s.s2.ok.c3: It is not (3, -2), which holds for every x.
y-m-54-10.s.s2.fail.c3: (3, -2) is an answer that holds for every x, so it is not a counterexample.
y-m-54-10.s.s2.explain: There are many pairs with a+b=1, such as (1,0), (0,1), (-2,3). Among them, the only one that holds for every x is (3,-2), and the rest do not match at x=2. Checking one value only checks one condition.
y-m-54-10.s.s3.prompt: Write a message to send to Seojin. Write, in words Seojin can understand, why checking only by putting in x=1 is not enough and what other check should be done.
y-m-54-10.s.s3.hint.0: Pick one (a, b) you made in s2, calculate both sides at x=1 and x=2, and write them in two lines.
y-m-54-10.s.s3.hint.1: Rewrite those two lines in an order that Seojin can follow along.
y-m-54-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the example (a, b) I made appear in the message at least once?
y-m-54-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does the message not only say that Seojin is wrong but also tell 'what more to do'?
y-m-54-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write it while recognizing what Seojin has already done (getting a+b=1)?
y-m-54-10.s.s3.model.0: What is right when you put in only x=1 is just the condition a+b=1. (0, 1) is also right at x=1, but at x=2 the left side is 1 and the right side is 4, so they differ. You have to put in another value like x=2 too and decide both a and b.
y-m-54-10.s.s3.model.1: If you check only one value, you get just one equation, a+b=1, so the conditions are not enough. If you put in one more different value, there are two equations, so you can decide a=3, b=-2.
y-m-54-10.s.s3.modelNote.1: It explained by the number of conditions instead of examples. It suggested the method of putting in one more different value.
